title: Claude Code adds experimental Code Mode that packs tool calls into one script, off by default
summary: Normally, when you ask Claude Code to edit several files or run a sequence of commands, it works one step at a time, stopping to read the result after each. With the new Code Mode, Claude writes a piece of JavaScript that chains those tool calls, runs them in parallel, and returns only the output it needs to read.
ai_summary: Claude Code has introduced an experimental Code Mode, off by default. The core change: before, Claude requested tools such as Bash, Read, and Edit one step at a time and read each result before deciding the next step. With Code Mode on, Claude writes a piece of JavaScript that chains multiple tool calls, runs some in parallel, feeds one result into the next, and returns only the output it needs to read. It suits tasks that repeat an edit across many files, need search results filtered before Claude reads them, or run several independent commands at once. Requirements: Claude Code v2.1.323 or later (v2.1.331 or later on cloud providers); a Claude subscription, Console account, or cloud provider such as Amazon Bedrock; and one of the models Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or Fable 5.2.
brief: Code Mode lets Claude write a piece of JavaScript that calls tools in batch: it can run calls in parallel, chain results, and return only the output Claude needs to read.
Experimental and off by default; waiting-mode code is capped at 10 minutes, and background-mode code can run for up to 2 hours.
Requirements: Claude Code v2.1.323 or later, cloud providers v2.1.331 or later, and models limited to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Fable 5.2.
To try it: set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE to 1, start claude, and confirm that you want it on.

sections.h: What it is: Claude calls tools by writing code

blocks.p: Code Mode is a new way for Claude Code to work. Before, Claude requested tool calls such as Bash, Read, and Edit one step at a time, and after each call it read the result before deciding what to do next. With Code Mode on, Claude instead writes a piece of JavaScript, and Claude Code runs that code in your session to make those tool calls.

It is still experimental and off by default, and Anthropic explicitly says it may change or be removed in any release. To share feedback, run /feedback. Treat the usage and requirements below as based on the current docs.

sections.h: How it differs: parallel calls, chained results, and only the needed output

blocks.p: The changes come down to a few things: one piece of code can run several commands in parallel, feed the result of one call into the next, and return only the part of the output Claude needs to read. Before, Claude had to wait through all of that round by round.

blocks.p: Anthropic gives an example: ask Claude to raise a retry limit. It might write code like the following — use `rg` to find files containing `retryPolicy`, take the first one, change `maxAttempts` from 3 to 5, then run `npm test`. The last line returns both the file path and the test output.

blocks.p: Anthropic suggests trying it on tasks that need many related tool calls; a one-off small edit doesn't need it.

sections.h: Requirements: version, account, model, and surface

blocks.p: The first requirement is version. Different setups need different minimum versions: the baseline is v2.1.323, and cloud providers, agent teams, mods, and telemetry settings each have a higher threshold.

fig.title: Minimum versions vary by setup
fig.subtitle: Use the Claude Code docs as the source of truth for version numbers; run claude update before starting.

blocks.p: Account or provider: a Claude subscription, a Console account, or a cloud provider such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. It can't be used through a gateway, or with Claude for Government.

Model: limited to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Fable 5.2. If you select the model by a deployment name or an application inference profile, ask whoever manages that name which model it actually points to.

Surface: it must be an interactive claude session in a terminal. The VS Code panel, the Desktop app, and cloud sessions won't work. At the organization level, you can't use the HIPAA configuration or zero data retention; on Windows, install Git for Windows first.

sections.h: How to turn it on, turn it off, and block it

blocks.p: Turning it on is simple: set the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE environment variable to 1, then start claude. The first time, it asks you to confirm; after the restart, a message near the top shows that Code Mode is on.

blocks.p: To turn it off: remove the variable from your shell, ~/.claude/settings.json, or any --settings file, or change its value to 0. If any one place has 0, Code Mode stays off.

To block it for your organization, add this variable with a value of 0 to managed settings. People already in a Code Mode session stay in it until they exit or restart Claude Code; after that, they can't resume those sessions.
One security detail: Claude Code ignores this variable in project settings files, so a repository you clone can't quietly turn on Code Mode for you.

sections.h: How permissions work: the classifier reviews each piece of code

blocks.p: Your permission mode decides how the code is checked. In auto and bypassPermissions modes, code can run from start to finish without a permission prompt. In auto mode, the classifier reviews each piece of code before it runs, not each tool call.

fig.title: The review target is the whole piece of code, not each tool call
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: the amber REPL runs the code; Bash, Edit, and MCP calls originate from it.
fig.note: In auto mode, the classifier reviews each piece of code; a PreToolUse hook matching REPL can read the JavaScript in tool_input.code.

blocks.p: Note: the classifier can't see values computed at runtime, such as a path taken from search output, so critical commands still depend on rules and hooks as a backstop. To control calls one by one, write deny / ask rules and PreToolUse hooks under the tool's usual name, such as Bash or an MCP tool name.
To review the code itself, write a PreToolUse hook that matches REPL and read the JavaScript from tool_input.code. Or add an ask rule for REPL so every piece of code waits for your approval.

Sandboxing: sandbox settings apply only to the shell commands the code runs. The JavaScript itself, plus its file, web, and MCP calls, runs outside the sandbox. To isolate those too, run Claude Code in a container or virtual machine.
One more detail: when no IDE is connected, a permission prompt may include a 1 minute 59 second countdown. If you don't answer in time, the call is automatically refused.

sections.h: Limitations: time, resuming, and unavailable features

blocks.p: First, runtime. In waiting mode, Claude waits for the code to finish before answering, and the code stops after 10 minutes. In background mode, you can keep talking while the code runs for up to 2 hours. Background mode must start from an auto or bypassPermissions session.

list: Resuming: a Code Mode session can be resumed only with Code Mode on. A session that ran with a Claude subscription or Console account can't be resumed on a cloud provider such as Amazon Bedrock.
Unavailable features: Remote Control, Claude in Chrome, and computer use can't be used at the same time.
You can't move the session to the Desktop app or turn it into a background session, and /fork can't start a background copy.
By default, if a PreToolUse hook doesn't finish, the tool call is refused.
Pricing or billing: the docs don't say whether this JavaScript is token-metered separately or how it is billed.
Timeline: when it leaves experimental status or becomes a stable feature isn't stated.
Performance: there are no published quantitative comparisons between Code Mode and normal mode on speed or token consumption.
Model coverage: whether more models will be supported later isn't stated.
Surface coverage: whether the VS Code panel or Desktop app will be supported isn't stated.
Time limits: whether the 10-minute and 2-hour caps will change later isn't stated.

blocks.p: The value: it compresses many related tool calls into one piece of code, reducing back-and-forth. It's especially useful for repetitive, batch, or parallelizable work.

The cost: it's an experimental feature that may change, with several requirements (version, account, model, terminal UI), and the permission-review logic changes, so you may need to reconfigure rules and hooks.

If you often have Claude Code edit code across many files and then run tests, it's worth trying. If you only make one-off small changes or rely on the VS Code panel or Desktop app, you can skip it for now. Team administrators can block it by setting 0 in managed settings and open it up once it stabilizes.
